Quick Check — Prior Probability P(Play = Yes) = 9/14. In probability and machine learning, this is called a "prior" probability. Why is it called "prior"? A. Because it was computed before computers existed B. Because it uses the first column of the data C. It's what you'd predict *before* looking at any features — your default belief based only on past outcomes D. It always equals 0.5

fragments.text: Answer: C. "Prior" means before seeing any evidence . It is your baseline belief, computed purely from how often each label appears in the data.

Quick Check — The Big Assumption In Exercise 3.1, you multiplied P(Sunny | Yes) × P(Hot | Yes). This multiplication is only mathematically valid under a specific assumption. What is it? A. Outlook and Temperature must have the same number of possible values B. Outlook and Temperature are *independent* given the label — knowing one doesn't tell you about the other (once you already know whether we played) C. The dataset must have at least 100 rows D. All feature probabilities must be greater than 0.5

fragments.text: Answer: B. This is the naive in Naive Bayes. We assume features are conditionally independent given the class label, so the joint probability factors into a product of individual probabilities. In reality features are often correlated, but the classifier works surprisingly well anyway.

slide_text: Part 5: The Zero-Frequency Problem Your algorithm has a fatal flaw. Let's find it and fix it.

Break Your Code Look at the data: Outlook = Overcast appears on days 3, 7, 12, 13. What is the Play label for all of those days? Now answer: What is P(Overcast | No)? If you try to predict for a new day with Outlook = Overcast and any other features, what happens to Score(No)? Is this a reasonable prediction? What if you had Overcast + Strong Wind + High Humidity — conditions that historically lean toward No?

Fix It: Laplace Smoothing The fix is beautifully simple: pretend you've seen every combination at least once. The idea: Instead of computing P(Overcast | No) = 0/5, add 1 to the numerator (pretend you saw one extra Overcast-No day) and add k to the denominator (where k is the number of possible values for that feature). For Outlook, k = 3 (Sunny, Overcast, Rainy). So: P_smooth(Overcast | No) = (0 + 1) / (5 + 3) = 1/8 = 0.125 Tasks: Compute P_smooth(Sunny | No) with k=3. Compare to the unsmoothed version. Write : [code block] Hint 1 The numerator is . The denominator is . Solution [code block]

[code block] Hint 1 To find k for a feature, collect all distinct values: . Then call instead of . Solution [code block]

Quick Check — Why Smoothing Works Laplace smoothing adds 1 to every count. What would happen if you added 1000 instead of 1? A. The classifier would become more accurate because it has more "data" B. Nothing would change — the relative ordering of scores stays the same C. All smoothed probabilities would approach 1/k (uniform) — the fake counts would overwhelm the real data, and the classifier would ignore the actual evidence D. Python would crash with an overflow error

fragments.text: Answer: C. With a huge smoothing value, the added fake counts dwarf the real counts, making every conditional probability close to 1/k. The classifier effectively forgets the training data. That is why the smoothing parameter (often called alpha) is typically kept small, like 1.

What About Continuous Features? Your classifier works with categorical features (Sunny, Rainy, etc.). But what if a feature is a number, like actual temperature (72°F, 85°F, etc.)? Why can't you directly count P(Temperature=72.3 | Yes)? (How many training rows have that exact value?) One approach: assume numerical features follow a bell curve (Gaussian distribution) within each class. Instead of counting, you'd compute the mean and standard deviation per class, then use the bell curve to get the probability. Another approach: bin the numbers into categories (e.g., Cold: 60, Mild: 60-80, Hot: 80) and use your existing categorical classifier. Try the binning approach on a dataset of your choice.
